pattern_candidates.description: A single entry point for client requests that routes registration, authentication, bike discovery, rental, payment, history, and admin operations to backend services.
source_driver_names: Cross-channel access for riders and administrators
pattern_candidates.rationale: The requirements involve multiple rider and administrator interactions over web and mobile clients. An API gateway can centralize authentication, routing, throttling, and policy enforcement while supporting a simpler client experience and consistent security controls.
limitations: Can become a bottleneck or single point of failure if not deployed redundantly
Adds operational complexity and must be kept aligned with service interfaces
Does not by itself solve domain decomposition or data consistency

pattern_candidates.description: A system decomposition approach where major business capabilities are implemented as independently deployable services such as identity, bike inventory, rental, payment, notification, and reporting.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
pattern_candidates.rationale: The system has distinct functional areas with different time and data characteristics: authentication, bike availability, reservations, payments, notifications, and reporting. Microservices can separate these concerns and allow independent scaling and evolution.
limitations: Introduces distributed-system complexity
Requires careful handling of inter-service consistency and observability
Can increase latency and deployment/operational overhead

pattern_candidates.description: A single deployable application organized into strict internal modules for identity, bike management, rental, payment, notification, and reporting boundaries.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
pattern_candidates.rationale: The requirements span many related business capabilities but do not yet prove that independent deployment is necessary. A modular monolith can preserve clear boundaries while avoiding distributed complexity, making it suitable when consistency and delivery simplicity are important.
limitations: May scale less flexibly than microservices for hotspots
Can evolve into a monolith if module boundaries are not enforced
Some availability and fault-isolation benefits are limited compared with distributed services

pattern_candidates.description: An asynchronous communication style where significant business events such as registration completion, bike reserved, bike released, rental expiring, and payment completed are published to interested consumers.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
pattern_candidates.rationale: Many requirements depend on state changes being propagated quickly and on time-based reactions such as expiry notices and reporting updates. Event-driven integration supports decoupling between rental, notification, availability, and analytics functions.
limitations: Adds eventual consistency and message-delivery complexity
Requires robust event design and idempotent consumers
Harder to reason about end-to-end flows than synchronous calls

pattern_candidates.description: A coordination pattern for multi-step business processes that spans several services or modules, using orchestration or choreography to manage long-running workflows and compensating actions.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
pattern_candidates.rationale: Bike selection, registration, payment, rental duration, and availability updates form a business process that may involve several components. A saga or process manager can coordinate these steps and define rollback/compensation when one step fails.
limitations: Increases workflow design complexity
Compensation logic may be approximate rather than fully transactional
Can be overkill if the system remains a modular monolith with local transactions

pattern_candidates.description: A separation of write-optimized commands from read-optimized queries, allowing availability, history, and reporting views to be modeled differently from transactional rental operations.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
Cross-channel access for riders and administrators
pattern_candidates.rationale: The system has distinct read concerns: nearby bike discovery, rider history, admin availability views, and aggregated usage reporting. CQRS can optimize these reads independently from rental and payment writes.
limitations: Introduces additional data synchronization and consistency concerns
Raises implementation complexity
May be unnecessary if query load is modest

pattern_candidates.description: A data ownership pattern in which each service or bounded context stores and manages its own data independently rather than sharing one central database.
source_driver_names: Real-time bike availability and location awareness
pattern_candidates.rationale: If the system is decomposed into separate services, independent data ownership helps isolate sensitive user, bike, payment, and reporting data and reduces coupling between capabilities.
limitations: Cross-service reporting and joins become harder
Requires integration patterns for synchronization and analytics
May complicate compliance auditing if data is widely distributed

pattern_candidates.description: An architecture that isolates core business logic from external systems by using ports and adapters for user interfaces, payment providers, messaging, mapping, and device capabilities.
pattern_candidates.rationale: The system must interact with clients, SMS/email providers, payment platforms, mapping/navigation services, and biometric input. Hexagonal architecture helps keep these integrations separate from core rental and identity logic.
limitations: Does not by itself define process orchestration or data distribution
Requires discipline to maintain adapter boundaries
May need to be combined with other patterns for scaling and events
